Treasury seasonality points to further weakness ahead:

The median monthly return on Treasuries during October was -0.71% between 2016 and 2025, the 2nd-worst monthly performance of the year.

This is only behind September’s median return of -0.86% over this period.

By comparison, November recorded the strongest median monthly return at +0.69%.

Meanwhile, the 10Y Treasury Note futures are down -2.85% so far this month, on track for their worst September performance since 2022.

At the same time, global government bonds are down -2.1%, putting them on track for their worst September performance since 2023.

History says Treasuries are likely to face more pressure.

"The founder is the asset class... The IPO is another financing event."

a16z's David George and Santiago Rodriguez on why the biggest companies are staying private:

Santiago: "If you look at the top six companies today, Anthropic, OpenAI, Databricks, Stripe, Waymo, and Revolut, by last round valuation, they add up to about $2.4 trillion."

"This is more than the combined market cap of IPOs we've seen in the last 10 years, excluding SpaceX, which adds up to $1.7 trillion."

David: "Especially for founder-led companies, one of the things that we've talked about and that I've written about is that the founder is the asset class at this point."

"The bet that we make, and part of the reason that it's been a benefit for some of these companies to remain private, is they can many times take bigger swings in the private markets that have longer duration paybacks."

"Zuck and Elon are kind of obvious exceptions to the rule in the public markets."

"You see it manifest in the numbers in companies like Databricks or Stripe: massive, massive new bets in new product areas, and you can see revenue acceleration that happens as a result."

"You can do that in the public markets, but it's gonna catch greater scrutiny. Meta's stock price at the nadir got below 100 bucks a share when people were very, very skeptical about their investments in AR/VR."

@DavidGeorge83 @santiago__rdz

tweets.text:
Meta launched an AI agent that scans your card statement and cancels the subscriptions you forgot about. Subscription stocks sold off on it. Then look at how small the target actually is.

The biggest category one of these bots can even touch is cell service at 0.77% of household spending. Streaming is 0.39%. Gyms, newspapers, cable, all under half a percent. Kill every one of them and consumption barely moves. That money gets spent somewhere else, it does not disappear.

The hit lands on the business model, not the consumer. These companies book anywhere from 14% to over 200% of their revenue on people forgetting to cancel. Take away the forgetting and that revenue walks out the door.

tweets.text:
🚨 In September, Korean exports reached $120.9 billion, up 83.5% year-on-year. Semiconductor exports surged 263% to $60.3 billion, and chips now account for nearly half of the country’s monthly exports. AI is clearly reshaping the macroeconomic data of a major industrial economy !

🇰🇷 As you all know, South Korea sits at the heart of the AI value chain through Samsung and SK Hynix that are essential for GPUs. As hyperscalers announce hundreds of billions of dollars in capex, part of that money ends up in Korean factories. No promises or valuations here, we are talking about components that are actually being produced, sold and exported. Out of $55 billion in additional exports compared with last year, close to $44 billion came from semiconductors alone. However, a large part of the move also comes from higher prices and a richer product mix as manufacturers shift toward more advanced and more profitable memory products. Nevertheless, demand is strong enough to create a major shock to revenues, margins, investment and Korea’s external trade.

⚠️ Meanwhile, this boom supports growth, corporate profits, tax revenues and the won, but it can also keep inflationary pressures elevated. The Bank of Korea has raised its 2026 growth forecast from 2.6% to 3.3% and is still tightening monetary policy. The more AI supports economic activity, the more it may help keep interest rates high, which in turn makes financing the next wave of data centers and infrastructure more expensive.

Let's be frank here, the boom is real.

*Bloomberg link: https://t.co/fNfFYvyqzv
